questions.question: In September 2024, who has been appointed as the new director general of the Narcotics Control Bureau?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Anurag Garg**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Anurag Garg** has been appointed as the new **Director General of the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB)** in **September 2024**. 
 
• The **Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB)** is the primary agency in India for combating drug trafficking and the abuse of illegal substances under the provisions of the **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985**. 
 
• Anurag Garg, an officer of the **Indian Police Service (IPS)**, has a distinguished career in handling various law enforcement and anti-drug operations, making him a suitable choice for this critical role. 
 
• The appointment comes at a time when the **Government of India** is strengthening its efforts to curb the menace of drug abuse and trafficking across the country. 
 
• As the Director General, Anurag Garg will oversee operations, policy implementation, and international collaboration to address drug-related crimes effectively. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB):** 
 
 
• The NCB was established in **1986** as the apex coordinating agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India. 
 
• Its primary function is the implementation of India’s **international obligations** with respect to drug control and the coordination between various central and state agencies. 
 
• The bureau focuses on intelligence sharing, conducting anti-drug operations, and prosecuting offenders involved in drug trafficking. 
 
 
 
• **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985:** 
 
 
• This is the principal legislation in India aimed at combating drug abuse and illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. 
 
• The act provides stringent provisions for the control and regulation of operations relating to narcotic drugs and substances. 
 
• It prescribes severe penalties for offences, including death or life imprisonment for certain cases. 
 
 
 
• **International Collaboration:** 
 
 
• NCB works closely with international organizations such as the **United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)** and foreign law enforcement agencies to combat transnational drug trafficking. 
 
• India is a signatory to various international treaties like the **Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961**, and the **Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988**. 
 
 
 
• **Key Challenges in Drug Control:** 
 
 
• The increasing use of the **dark web** and **cryptocurrencies** for drug transactions has become a significant challenge for law enforcement agencies. 
 
• India's geographical location makes it vulnerable to drug trafficking from the **Golden Crescent** and **Golden Triangle** regions. 
 
• Strengthening inter-agency coordination and capacity building is crucial for addressing these challenges effectively. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Anurag Garg's Appointment:** 
 
 
• He is an experienced officer with extensive knowledge and expertise in counter-narcotics operations and law enforcement mechanisms. 
 
• His leadership is expected to bring about impactful reforms and improvements in the functioning of the Narcotics Control Bureau. 
 
 
 
• **NCB's Role in India:** 
 
 
• The agency not only conducts seizures and arrests but also plays a critical role in spreading awareness about the adverse effects of drug abuse through campaigns and programs. 
 
• It collaborates with other government agencies like the **Central Bureau of Narcotics** and the **Directorate of Revenue Intelligence** for joint operations. 
 
 
 
• **Impact of Drug Abuse:** 
 
 
• Drug abuse leads to severe health, social, and economic consequences, impacting individuals, families, and communities. 
 
• It is also linked to organized crimes, terrorism, and human trafficking, necessitating stringent measures for its control.

questions.question: Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban 2.0, approved in August 2024 aims to provide housing subsidies to which group?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Urban poor and middle-class families**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban 2.0 (PMAY-U 2.0)** was approved in **August 2024** as a continuation of the original PMAY-U scheme aimed at ensuring housing for all by targeting the **urban poor and middle-class families**.
 
• The scheme provides **subsidies on housing** for eligible beneficiaries, enabling them to purchase, construct, or upgrade houses in urban areas.
 
• Under PMAY-U 2.0, **Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS)** continues to play a pivotal role in offering interest subsidies on home loans to economically weaker sections (EWS), low-income groups (LIG), and middle-income groups (MIG).
 
• The scheme is specifically designed to address the housing deficit in urban areas, where **rapid urbanization** has led to a significant shortage of affordable housing options.
 
• PMAY-U 2.0 aligns with the government’s vision of providing **‘Housing for All’ by 2024**, ensuring inclusion and socio-economic upliftment of urban populations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Eligibility Criteria:**

 
 
• Urban poor, including individuals from **Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)**, with an annual income of up to **₹3 lakh**.
 
• Low-income groups (LIG) with an annual income between **₹3 lakh and ₹6 lakh**.
 
• Middle-income groups (MIG) with incomes up to **₹18 lakh** are also eligible for benefits under the **Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS)**.
 
 
 
• **Subsidy Details:**
 
 
• Interest subsidies range from **3% to 6.5%**, depending on the income group and loan amount.
 
• The maximum loan amount eligible for subsidy can go up to **₹12 lakh** for MIG households.
 
 
 
• **Implementation:**
 
 
• The scheme is implemented by **Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)**, state governments, and private developers in partnership with financial institutions.
 
• Monitoring and funding are overseen by the **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs**.
 
 
 
• **Achievements:**
 
 
• Under the original PMAY-U, over **1.2 crore houses** were sanctioned, and more than **75 lakh houses** were completed as of 2023.
 
• PMAY-U 2.0 aims to accelerate this progress, focusing on reducing urban housing shortages further.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 2: All women-headed households:** While PMAY-U 2.0 emphasizes empowering women, particularly by making house ownership mandatory in the names of women, the scheme is not exclusively for women-headed households.
 
• **Option 3: MSME workers in urban slums:** Although PMAY-U 2.0 covers urban slums, it does not exclusively target **MSME workers**; it targets all eligible urban poor and middle-class families.
 
• **Option 4: Airline industry employees:** This option is irrelevant as the scheme is not industry-specific and focuses on housing for the urban poor and middle-class families.

questions.question: Which of the Indian state/union territory achieved 1st rank in India Electric Mobility Index 2024?

__
 
• **Delhi** has achieved the **1st rank in the India Electric Mobility Index (IEMI) 2024**, showcasing its leadership in promoting electric mobility and sustainable transportation.
 
• The **India Electric Mobility Index** is a comprehensive assessment tool developed to evaluate the performance of Indian states and Union Territories (UTs) in the adoption and promotion of **electric vehicles (EVs)**.
 
• Delhi has excelled in various parameters, including **policy implementation, EV infrastructure development, and adoption of EVs** by the public.
 
• The city's **Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2020** has been instrumental in encouraging EV adoption by providing subsidies, tax incentives, and promoting charging infrastructure.
 
• Delhi's efforts align with India's broader goal of achieving **30% EV penetration by 2030**, as part of its commitment to reducing carbon emissions and promoting sustainable urban mobility.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **India Electric Mobility Index (IEMI):**
 
 
• The IEMI evaluates the performance of states and UTs on their efforts to promote **electric mobility**, focusing on parameters like **policy framework, infrastructure, adoption rates, and awareness campaigns**.
 
• The index is an initiative by **government institutions and think tanks** to encourage healthy competition among states/UTs and accelerate EV adoption.
 
 
 
• **Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2020:**
 
 
• Launched in **August 2020**, the policy focuses on making Delhi the **EV capital of India**.
 
• Key features include **purchase incentives, scrapping incentives**, and the development of **charging infrastructure**.
 
• The policy aims to achieve **25% EV registration by 2024**.
 
 
 
• **India's EV Goals:**
 
 
• India has set a target of **30% EV penetration by 2030** to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and curb carbon emissions.
 
• Initiatives like the **Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (FAME)** scheme provide financial support for EV adoption.

• **Haryana:** Focused on building EV infrastructure but has not matched Delhi's progress.

• **FAME India Scheme:**
 
 
• The **Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (FAME)** scheme was launched in **2015** to promote EV adoption in India.
 
• Under the second phase of the scheme, the government allocated **₹10,000 crore** to provide subsidies for EVs and develop charging infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Benefits of EV Adoption:**
 
 
• **Reduces air pollution:** EVs produce zero tailpipe emissions, contributing to cleaner air quality.
 
• **Energy security:** Promotes the use of renewable energy and reduces dependence on imported oil.
 
• **Cost savings:** EVs have lower running costs compared to conventional fuel vehicles.

questions.question: The Kadbanwadi grassland is in____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Maharashtra**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **Kadbanwadi grassland** is located in the state of **Maharashtra**, India. It is a notable ecological area known for its rich biodiversity and grassland ecosystems. 

• This grassland is part of the semi-arid zone of Maharashtra, characterized by its dry climate and unique vegetation that supports various species of flora and fauna. 

• **Kadbanwadi** is situated in the **Pune district** of Maharashtra, and it is a significant area for grazing and local livelihoods. 

• Grasslands like Kadbanwadi play a critical role in maintaining ecological balance, serving as habitats for numerous species and acting as carbon sinks. 

• These grasslands are often used for **agricultural activities** and livestock grazing, making them essential for the rural economy of the region. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Grasslands in India:** 
 

• Grasslands are a critical ecological asset, covering approximately **24% of India’s geographical area**. 

• India's grasslands are classified into various types, such as **tropical, temperate, and alpine**, based on climatic conditions and geographical location. 

• They are vital for supporting **biodiversity**, including herbivores like deer and livestock such as cattle, sheep, and goats. 
 
 

• **Importance of Grasslands:** 
 

• Grasslands are essential for maintaining the **balance of ecosystems** by acting as habitats for wildlife and regulating local climates. 

• They serve as **grazing grounds** for livestock, contributing significantly to the livelihoods of pastoral communities. 

• Grasslands help in **soil conservation** by preventing erosion and maintaining soil fertility. 
 
 

• **Challenges faced by Grasslands:** 
 

• Grasslands are under threat due to **urbanization**, industrialization, and conversion into agricultural lands. 

• Overgrazing and deforestation also lead to **degradation** of grassland ecosystems, affecting their biodiversity. 

• Climate change poses a significant risk, altering the vegetation patterns and productivity of these areas. 
 
 

• **Conservation Efforts:** 
 

• The Indian government and various environmental organizations are working towards **grassland conservation** by implementing sustainable grazing practices. 

• Projects like the **National Afforestation Programme** aim to restore degraded grasslands and promote biodiversity. 

• Community participation and awareness programs are being conducted to ensure the protection of these critical ecosystems. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Other Grassland Areas in India:** 
 

• The **Banni grasslands** in Gujarat are among the largest tropical grasslands in Asia. 

• The **Shola grasslands** of the Western Ghats are known for their unique biodiversity and endemic species. 

• The **Terai grasslands** of northern India are home to iconic species like the Bengal tiger and Indian rhinoceros. 
 
 

• **Global Importance:** 
 

• Grasslands are often referred to as the **“lungs of the Earth”** due to their role in carbon sequestration. 

• They are part of the global efforts to combat **climate change** through preservation and restoration strategies.

questions.question: Who is the author of the book 'The Namesake'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jhumpa Lahiri**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Jhumpa Lahiri** is the author of the novel **"The Namesake"**, which was published in **2003**. 
 
• The book explores themes of **identity, cultural assimilation, and the immigrant experience**, particularly focusing on the life of a Bengali family in the United States. 
 
• **"The Namesake"** is Jhumpa Lahiri's first novel, following her Pulitzer Prize-winning short story collection **"Interpreter of Maladies" (1999)**. 
 
• The protagonist of the novel, **Gogol Ganguli**, struggles to reconcile his Indian heritage with his American upbringing, making the book a poignant tale of identity and belonging. 
 
• A film adaptation of **"The Namesake"**, directed by **Mira Nair**, was released in **2006**, further popularizing the book. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

 
 
• **Jhumpa Lahiri's Background:** 
 
 
• Jhumpa Lahiri was born in **London** to Bengali parents and later moved to the **United States**. 
 
• She is known for her exploration of themes related to **diaspora, identity, and family dynamics**. 
 
• Lahiri has received numerous accolades, including the **Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2000** for her debut short story collection "Interpreter of Maladies." 
 
 
 
• **About "The Namesake":** 
 
 
• The title **"The Namesake"** refers to the protagonist's name, **Gogol**, which holds cultural and emotional significance for his family. 
 
• The novel addresses the complexities of **intergenerational and cross-cultural relationships**. 
 
• It is considered a modern classic and is often studied in literature courses for its exploration of immigrant identity. 
 
 
 
• **Other Works by Jhumpa Lahiri:** 
 
 
• **"Interpreter of Maladies" (1999):** A collection of short stories that earned her the Pulitzer Prize. 
 
• **"Unaccustomed Earth" (2008):** Another acclaimed collection of short stories. 
 
• **"In Other Words" (2016):** A memoir written in Italian, reflecting her love for the language and culture of Italy. 
 
 
 
• **Other Options:** 
 
 
• **Arundhati Roy:** Author of "The God of Small Things," which won the Booker Prize in 1997. 
 
• **Satyajit Ray:** Renowned filmmaker and writer, known for his Feluda series in Bengali literature. 
 
• **Arun Joshi:** Known for novels like "The Strange Case of Billy Biswas" and "The Apprentice."

questions.question: -What is the change of state from liquid to solid at atmospheric pressure known as?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Solidification**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Solidification** is the process by which a substance changes its state from a **liquid to a solid**. This typically occurs when the liquid is cooled to its freezing point.
 
• The freezing point is the temperature at which the liquid and solid phases of a substance coexist in equilibrium. For water, this temperature is **0°C (273.15 K)** at standard atmospheric pressure.
 
• In the case of solidification, the **molecules of the liquid lose kinetic energy** due to cooling. As a result, they slow down and arrange themselves into a fixed, orderly structure, forming a solid.
 
• Solidification is an **exothermic process**, meaning it releases heat as the liquid transitions into a solid state.
 
• This process is a key principle in various natural phenomena and industrial applications, such as the formation of ice, the casting of metals, and the crystallization of substances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Deposition:** 
 
 
• Deposition is the **direct change of state from gas to solid** without passing through the liquid phase.
 
• An example of deposition is the formation of frost, where water vapor in the air turns directly into ice on cold surfaces.
 
 
 
• **Sublimation:**
 
 
• Sublimation refers to the change of state from a **solid to a gas** without passing through the liquid phase.
 
• An example of sublimation is the transformation of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) directly into carbon dioxide gas.
 
 
 
• **Evaporation:**
 
 
• Evaporation is the process where a liquid changes to a gas at a temperature **below its boiling point**.
 
• It occurs at the surface of the liquid and is responsible for phenomena like drying of clothes and the cooling effect of sweat.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Solidification:**
 
 
• **Metal casting:** The process of shaping metals involves pouring molten metal into molds and allowing it to solidify.
 
• **Ice formation:** Solidification occurs naturally when water is cooled below its freezing point, forming ice.
 
• **Crystallization:** In industries, solidification is used to extract pure solid crystals from a solution.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Freezing vs. Solidification:** 
 
 
• Freezing is a specific type of solidification that occurs when a liquid turns into a solid at its freezing point.
 
• Solidification is a more general term that can apply to any liquid turning into a solid, regardless of the temperature or conditions.
 
 
 
• **Latent Heat of Fusion:**
 
 
• The **latent heat of fusion** is the amount of heat energy required to change a unit mass of a substance from solid to liquid (or vice versa) at constant temperature.
 
• For water, the latent heat of fusion is approximately **334 J/g**.
 
 
 
• **Phase Changes and Thermodynamics:**
 
 
• All phase changes, including solidification, involve the transfer of energy in the form of heat.
 
• During solidification, the system releases heat to its surroundings, which is why it is classified as an **exothermic process**.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correct regarding law of conservation of energy?

I. Energy can only be converted from one form to another.

II. Energy can be easily destroyed.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I.**__
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Law of Conservation of Energy:** It states that **energy cannot be created or destroyed**, but can only be converted from one form to another. For example, chemical energy in food is converted into kinetic energy when we move. *Hence, statement I is correct.* 
 
• **Energy Transformation:** The principle allows the transformation of energy forms such as **mechanical, thermal, chemical, electrical, and nuclear energy**. These transformations are essential for various physical processes. 
 
• **Incorrect Interpretation:** Statement II claims that energy can be easily destroyed, which violates the law of conservation of energy. Energy cannot be destroyed; it only changes form or dissipates into less useful forms such as heat. *Hence, statement II is incorrect.* 
 
• Examples of energy conservation include the functioning of machines, the photosynthesis process in plants, and the operation of electrical appliances where input energy is converted to a useful form. 
 
• The principle is fundamental to physics and engineering, forming the basis for understanding energy systems across various domains. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Definition:** The law of conservation of energy is a fundamental principle in physics stating that the **total energy in an isolated system remains constant over time**, regardless of the transformations it undergoes. 
 
• **Historical Background:** The concept was first introduced by **Émilie du Châtelet** in the 18th century and later refined by **James Joule** and others during the Industrial Revolution. 
 
• **Applications:** 
 
 
• **In Thermodynamics:** The first law of thermodynamics is based on energy conservation, stating that the energy added to a system is equal to the sum of its increase in internal energy and the work done by the system. 
 
• **In Mechanical Systems:** Conservation of mechanical energy allows engineers to design efficient engines, turbines, and machines. 
 
• **In Electrical Systems:** It is used in calculating power consumption and designing circuits for minimal energy loss. 
 
 
 
• **Real-Life Examples:** 
 
 
• **Hydroelectric Power Plants:** Potential energy of water stored in dams is converted into kinetic energy and then into electrical energy. 
 
• **Solar Panels:** Solar energy is transformed into electrical energy through photovoltaic cells. 
 
• **Automobiles:** Chemical energy in fuel is converted into mechanical energy to power the vehicle. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Energy Conversion Examples:** 
 
 
• **Pendulum:** A pendulum demonstrates the conversion of potential energy to kinetic energy and vice versa. 
 
• **Electric Bulbs:** Electrical energy is converted into light and heat energy. 
 
 
 
• **Relation to Modern Physics:** Einstein’s equation **E=mc²** demonstrates the equivalence of energy and mass, expanding the scope of energy conservation. 
 
• **In Cosmology:** Conservation laws play a significant role in understanding the dynamics of the universe, including dark energy and matter.

questions.question: The 'ossification test' is used to determine the__________. of a person.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Age**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• The **ossification test** is a scientific method used to determine the **age of a person** by studying the development and fusion of bones. 
 
• This test is based on the principle that the **human skeleton undergoes predictable changes** as a person grows older, with certain bones fusing at specific ages. 
 
• The process of **ossification**, or bone formation, begins in the fetus and continues into early adulthood, making it a reliable marker for age estimation. 
 
• It is commonly used in **forensic investigations**, **legal disputes** (such as determining the age of juveniles), and in fields like **anthropology** and **archaeology**. 
 
• The test typically involves X-ray imaging of bones like the **clavicle**, **pelvis**, **wrists**, and **long bones**, as these are key indicators of age-specific bone fusion patterns.

• **Primary ossification:** This process begins during the fetal stage and involves the formation of the bone's diaphysis (shaft). 
 
• **Secondary ossification:** This occurs after birth and includes the development of the epiphysis (ends of long bones). 
 
• The fusion of epiphyseal plates (growth plates) occurs at specific ages, providing key indicators for age estimation. 
 
 
 
• **Applications of Ossification Test:** 
 
 
• **Forensic Science:** Used to determine the age of unidentified bodies or suspects in legal cases. 
 
• **Sports:** Helps verify the age of athletes in age-restricted competitions. 
 
• **Legal Disputes:** Often employed in cases involving child labor, juvenile crime, and adoption to ascertain the true age of individuals. 
 
 
 
• **Accuracy:** 
 
 
• The ossification test is generally accurate but may vary slightly depending on factors like **genetics**, **nutrition**, and **environmental conditions**.

• **Limitations:**

• **Bone Fusion Timelines:** 
 
 
• The **clavicle** is one of the last bones to ossify, completing its fusion around the age of 25. 
 
• In children, the **wrists** and **knees** are key indicators of bone age, as they show early ossification patterns. 
 
 
 
• **Global Relevance:** 
 
 
• The ossification test is recognized worldwide for its utility in forensic and legal contexts. 
 
• Different countries may have specific guidelines or protocols for conducting the test, ensuring its reliability and validity in various contexts.

questions.question: In progressive income taxation___________.

options.text: higher income leads to a higher tax rate
everyone pays the same tax rate
lower income leads to a higher tax rate
higher income leads to a lower tax rate

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**In progressive income taxation, higher income leads to a higher tax rate.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Progressive taxation** is a system in which the tax rate increases as the taxable income increases, ensuring that individuals with higher earnings contribute a larger percentage of their income in taxes.
 
• This system is based on the principle of **equity**, where those who earn more are expected to pay proportionately more to support societal needs.
 
• Progressive tax structures often involve **tax brackets**, where income is divided into ranges, and each range is taxed at a specific rate. For example, income below a certain threshold may be taxed at 10%, while higher income ranges are taxed at 20%, 30%, etc.
 
• This approach helps to reduce income inequality by redistributing wealth and funding essential services such as **education, healthcare, and infrastructure**.
 
• Examples of progressive taxes include **income tax in many countries**, such as India, the United States, and the United Kingdom. In contrast to flat taxes, progressive taxes are designed to be fairer to lower-income earners.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Flat Taxation:** 
 
• In a flat tax system, **everyone pays the same tax rate**, regardless of their income level. This structure is simpler but can disproportionately affect low-income individuals.
 
• Examples of flat tax systems include **corporate tax rates** in some countries and certain consumption taxes.
 
 
• **Regressive Taxation:** 
 
• In a regressive tax system, the **tax rate decreases as income increases**, resulting in a higher burden on lower-income individuals.
 
• Examples include **sales taxes or excise taxes**, which represent a larger proportion of income for poorer individuals.
 
 
• **Application of Progressive Taxation:** 
 
• Progressive taxation is widely used in countries with social welfare systems to promote **economic stability** and reduce disparities between rich and poor.
 
• For instance, in the United States, federal income tax follows a progressive model with **seven tax brackets**, ranging from 10% to 37% based on income levels.
 
 
• **Historical Context:** 
 
• Progressive taxation was first proposed by **Adam Smith** in his book "The Wealth of Nations" (1776) as a fair way to collect revenue.
 
• It was implemented in countries like the United Kingdom in **1799** and the United States in **1913**.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Benefits of Progressive Taxation:** 
 
• It **reduces income inequality** by redistributing wealth through higher taxes on the rich.
 
• Encourages economic stability by funding public services essential for societal welfare.
 
• Promotes the principle of **social justice**, ensuring that those with greater financial capacity contribute more.
 
 
• **Challenges:** 
 
• Progressive taxation can discourage **high earners** from investing or working harder due to higher tax burdens.
 
• Tax evasion and avoidance practices can undermine the effectiveness of progressive tax systems.
 
• Administrative complexity in calculating and enforcing tax brackets.
 
</ul

questions.question: In which year the SEBI formulated the 'Insider Trading Regulations'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1992**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 
__ 

• **Insider Trading Regulations** were first formulated by the **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)** in the year **1992**. These regulations aimed to curb insider trading practices, ensuring fair and transparent functioning of the securities market. 

• The regulations are officially called the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 1992**. 

• These regulations were enacted under the powers conferred by the **SEBI Act of 1992**, which gave SEBI the authority to regulate activities in the securities market. 

• Insider trading refers to the trading of securities by individuals or entities having **privileged access to non-public, material information** about the company. 

• The 1992 regulations were a significant step toward **strengthening investor protection** and ensuring market integrity by preventing the misuse of insider information. 

• These regulations have undergone several amendments over the years to incorporate evolving market dynamics, the latest being the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **About SEBI:** 
 

• The **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)** was established in **1988** and was given statutory powers in **1992** under the SEBI Act. 

• SEBI is responsible for **regulating the securities market**, protecting investor interests, and promoting the development of the stock market in India. 

• It oversees various market participants, including **stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds**, and other intermediaries. 
 
 

• **Features of SEBI Insider Trading Regulations:** 
 

• The regulations define **“insider”** as a person who has access to **unpublished price-sensitive information** about securities. 

• They prohibit insiders from **trading securities** while in possession of such information. 

• Penalties under the regulations include **monetary fines and imprisonment** as per provisions of the SEBI Act. 
 
 

• **Amendments to the Regulations:** 
 

• In **2015**, SEBI introduced revised regulations under the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**. 

• The revised regulations focused on concepts like **Chinese Walls**, which aim to restrict the flow of sensitive information within organizations. 

• They also introduced measures for **automated monitoring** and reporting of insider trading cases using technology. 
 
 

• **Global Relevance:** 
 

• Insider trading is prohibited globally, with similar regulations in countries like the **USA (under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934)** and the **UK (under the Criminal Justice Act 1993)**. 

• International bodies such as the **International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO)** also promote best practices to address insider trading globally. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **1992 SEBI Act:** 
 

• The SEBI Act of **1992** gave SEBI **statutory powers** to regulate the securities market and prevent malpractices like insider trading. 

• The act also empowered SEBI to enforce penalties and take legal actions against violators. 
 
 

• **Role of Insider Trading Regulations:** 
 

• The regulations aim to enhance **investor confidence** by ensuring transparency and fairness in trading practices. 

• They play a crucial role in maintaining the **integrity of financial markets** and safeguarding small investors from exploitation. 
 
 

• **Recent Developments:** 
 

• SEBI has introduced measures like **online reporting systems**, whistleblower mechanisms, and stricter penalties for insider trading violations. 

• It has been focusing on leveraging **technology and data analytics** to detect suspicious trading activities more efficiently.

questions.question: The Vice President of India can be removed from office by__________.

options.text: Resolution passed by the Council of States and agreed to by the House of the People
Resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament with one-thirds majority
The President on the advice of the Prime Minister

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Resolution passed by the Council of States and agreed to by the House of the People**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Article 67** of the Constitution of India states that the **Vice President of India** can be removed from office through a **resolution passed by the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and agreed to by the House of the People (Lok Sabha).** 

• The resolution must be passed in the **Rajya Sabha by an absolute majority** (more than half of the total members) and then agreed to by the **Lok Sabha.** 

• The process for removal requires the resolution to be introduced after a **14-day prior notice** signed by at least 50 members of the Rajya Sabha. 

• This provision ensures that the removal of the Vice President is conducted with due deliberation, maintaining the dignity of the office. 

• The Vice President can only be removed for reasons that align with the rules and procedures of parliamentary democracy; arbitrary removal is not permitted. *Hence, the correct answer is Resolution passed by the Council of States and agreed to by the House of the People.* 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Role of the Vice President:** 
 

• The Vice President of India is the **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**. 

• He/she acts as the second-highest constitutional office in India and assists the President in case of absence or resignation. 

• The term of the Vice President is **five years**, but he/she can continue in office until the successor assumes charge. 
 
 

• **Election Process:** 
 

• The Vice President is elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of the **members of both Houses of Parliament**. 

• The election is conducted through a **single transferable vote system** and is by secret ballot. 

• The candidate must be a citizen of India, at least **35 years old**, and qualified to be a member of the Rajya Sabha. 
 
 

• **Removal Procedure:** 
 

• The Vice President can be removed through a resolution passed in the Rajya Sabha and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, as per **Article 67**. 

• A **14-day notice** is mandatory before moving the resolution. 

• Unlike the President, the Vice President does not face impeachment; the removal process is simpler but requires legislative consensus. 
 
 

• **Important Articles:** 
 

• **Article 63:** Specifies that there shall be a Vice President of India. 

• **Article 64:** States the role of the Vice President as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. 

• **Article 66:** Deals with the election of the Vice President. 

• **Article 67:** Provides for the removal of the Vice President. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Comparison with Presidential Impeachment:** 
 

• The **President** of India can be removed through an impeachment process, which is more complex and requires charges to be proved. 

• The **Vice President**, however, is removed through a resolution, making the process less rigorous. 
 
 

• **Historical Context:** 
 

• Since the establishment of the office, no Vice President of India has been removed from office. 

• This reflects the stability of the constitutional framework and the respect for the office. 
 
 

• **Significance of the Office:** 
 

• The Vice President ensures the smooth functioning of the Rajya Sabha and acts as a crucial link in legislative processes. 

• He/she plays a key role in maintaining parliamentary decorum and resolving disputes within the Rajya Sabha.

• **Land reforms in Kerala:** Kerala implemented one of the most successful land reform programs in India after independence. The **Kerala Land Reforms Act** (1969) abolished tenancy and ensured ownership rights for tenants. This led to significant socio-economic changes in the state, reducing inequality and empowering marginalized communities. *Hence, Kerala's reforms were successful.*
 
• **Land reforms in West Bengal:** West Bengal introduced land reforms under the leadership of the **Left Front government**. Programs like **"Operation Barga"** provided ownership rights to sharecroppers and improved agricultural productivity. These initiatives enhanced rural livelihoods and reduced exploitation. *Thus, West Bengal's reforms were also successful.*
 
• Both Kerala and West Bengal adopted strategies that prioritized redistribution of land, tenant rights, and reduction of landlord exploitation. Their efforts serve as models for land reform in India.
 
• Land reforms in these states contributed to a reduction in rural poverty and improved access to resources for marginalized communities.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both I and II.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Land reforms in India:**
 
 
• Land reforms refer to the redistribution of land to ensure equity in ownership and access to land resources.
 
• Post-independence, India introduced measures such as the abolition of **zamindari system**, tenancy reforms, and ceilings on land holdings.
 
• The objective was to address the issues of inequality, poverty, and exploitation in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Kerala Land Reforms Act:**
 
 
• The **Kerala Land Reforms Act** (1969) abolished tenancy and granted ownership rights to tenants.
 
• It also imposed ceilings on land holdings and distributed surplus land to the landless.
 
• This initiative significantly reduced the influence of landlords and improved rural socio-economic conditions.
 
 
 
• **Operation Barga in West Bengal:**
 
 
• Initiated in the late **1970s**, Operation Barga aimed to provide tenancy rights to sharecroppers.
 
• Under this program, sharecroppers were registered and granted legal rights to cultivate the land.
 
• This led to increased agricultural productivity and reduced exploitation by landlords.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in land reforms:**
 
 
• Despite success in some states, land reforms in India faced challenges such as poor implementation, resistance from landlords, and lack of political will.
 
• Several states still struggle with issues of land inequality and exploitation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• Land reforms have proven instrumental in reducing poverty and inequality in rural India.
 
• States like Kerala and West Bengal highlight how effective policies can transform agrarian economies.
 
• However, uneven implementation across states remains a concern.
 
 
 
• **Articles of the Constitution related to land reforms:**

questions.question: In humans, what is the value of normal systolic and diastolic blood pressure respectively?

options.text: 75 mm Hg and 60 mm Hg respectively
80 mm Hg and 70 mm Hg respectively
100 mm Hg and 95 mm Hg respectively
​120 mm Hg and 80 mm Hg respectively

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**120 mm Hg and 80 mm Hg respectively**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• The **normal systolic blood pressure** in humans is **120 mm Hg**, while the **normal diastolic blood pressure** is **80 mm Hg**. These values are considered standard for a healthy adult. 
 
• **Systolic blood pressure** is the pressure exerted on the walls of the arteries when the heart contracts and pumps blood into the circulation. 
 
• **Diastolic blood pressure** is the pressure in the arteries when the heart is at rest between beats and filling with blood. 
 
• The measurement of blood pressure is expressed in millimeters of mercury (**mm Hg**), a unit that indicates the force exerted by the blood on the walls of blood vessels. 
 
• A reading of **120/80 mm Hg** is often referred to as the **gold standard** for cardiovascular health, reflecting optimal functioning of the circulatory system. 
 
• Values above 140/90 mm Hg are generally categorized as **hypertension**, while values below 90/60 mm Hg are classified as **hypotension**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 
 
• **Understanding Systolic and Diastolic Pressure:** 
 
 
• **Systolic Pressure:** It represents the peak pressure in the arteries during the heartbeat when the heart's ventricles contract. 
 
• **Diastolic Pressure:** It represents the lowest pressure in the arteries when the heart is resting between beats. 
 
• Both readings are vital to determine the overall health of the heart and blood vessels. 
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Blood Pressure:** 
 
 
• **Age:** Blood pressure tends to rise with age due to arterial stiffness. 
 
• **Lifestyle:** Sedentary habits, high-sodium diets, and obesity can increase blood pressure, while regular exercise and a balanced diet can help maintain normal levels. 
 
• **Stress:** Chronic stress can lead to elevated blood pressure over time. 
 
• **Genetics:** A family history of hypertension increases an individual’s risk. 
 
 
 
• **Importance of Monitoring Blood Pressure:** 
 
 
• Regular monitoring helps detect **hypertension**, which is a major risk factor for heart disease and stroke. 
 
• It aids in managing chronic conditions like **diabetes**, **kidney disease**, and other cardiovascular disorders. 
 
• Early detection allows for timely interventions such as lifestyle changes and medication. 
 
 
 
• **Categories of Blood Pressure:** 
 
 
• **Normal:** Less than 120/80 mm Hg. 
 
• **Elevated:** Systolic between 120-129 mm Hg and diastolic less than 80 mm Hg. 
 
• **Hypertension Stage 1:** Systolic between 130-139 mm Hg or diastolic between 80-89 mm Hg. 
 
• **Hypertension Stage 2:** Systolic 140 mm Hg or higher or diastolic 90 mm Hg or higher. 
 
 
 
• **Measurement of Blood Pressure:** 
 
 
• A **sphygmomanometer** is commonly used to measure blood pressure. 
 
• It involves a cuff that is wrapped around the arm and inflated to constrict blood flow, followed by a gradual release to measure systolic and diastolic pressures.
